module.title: Making Plans, Suggestions & Invitations
module.objective: Make, accept, and politely decline invitations and social plans using 'Would you like to...?' and 'Let's'.

subModules.title: Reading Mission: Plans, Suggestions & Invitations in Action
subModules.grammarFocus: Would you like to + base verb, Let's + base verb, Why don't we + base verb, and polite responses
subModules.vocabularyFocus: Invitations, suggestions, plans, accepting and declining politely, time and place expressions

content.summary: Welcome to your Reading Mission! In this lesson, you will read a short, fun conversation between friends who are making plans for the weekend. You will see how people invite each other, make suggestions, and politely accept or decline invitations in everyday English. By the end of this mission, you will feel confident reading messages and conversations about plans and invitations. Let's get started!

linguisticTarget.grammar: Invitation patterns: 'Would you like to + base verb?', suggestion patterns: 'Let's + base verb' and 'Why don't we + base verb?', and polite responses for accepting ('I'd love to!', 'That sounds great!', 'Sure, why not?') and declining ('I'm sorry, I'm busy', 'I'd love to, but I can't', 'Maybe another time?').
linguisticTarget.vocabulary: Words and phrases related to invitations, suggestions, plans, appointments, time expressions (this weekend, on Saturday, at 5 PM), and social activities (have dinner, watch a movie, go to a party).
linguisticTarget.readingStrategy: First, skim the passage quickly to understand the main idea: Who is talking? What are they planning? Then, scan for specific details like times, places, and whether people accept or decline invitations.

learningObjectives: Understand the main idea of a short A1 conversation about making plans and invitations.
Identify key details including who invites whom, what activity is suggested, and when and where it happens.
Recognize invitation patterns such as 'Would you like to...?', 'Let's...', and 'Why don't we...?' in context.
Distinguish between accepting and declining responses in a polite conversation.
Build confidence reading natural, everyday English about social plans.

contextWarmup.prompt: Your friend sends you this message: 'Would you like to have lunch with me on Saturday?' What is your friend doing?
options: Inviting you to eat together
Asking about your favourite food
Telling you about a restaurant
contextWarmup.explanation: The phrase 'Would you like to have lunch with me?' is an invitation. Your friend is asking you to eat together on Saturday. The pattern 'Would you like to + verb' is used to politely invite someone to do something.

rules: Use 'Would you like to + base verb?' to politely invite someone. Example: 'Would you like to come to my party?' Always use the base form of the verb (come, go, have) — never add '-ing' or '-s'.
Use 'Let's + base verb' to make a friendly suggestion that includes yourself. Example: 'Let's meet at the café.' Do NOT add 'to' after 'Let's' — say 'Let's go', not 'Let's to go'.
Use 'Why don't we + base verb?' to suggest an activity as a question. Example: 'Why don't we watch a movie tonight?' This is a friendly way to propose an idea.
To accept an invitation politely, say: 'I'd love to!', 'That sounds great!', 'Sure, why not?', or 'Yes, that would be nice!'
To decline an invitation politely, say: 'I'm sorry, I'm busy.', 'I'd love to, but I can't.', or 'Maybe another time?' Always be kind when you say no.

commonTrap.explanation: Many beginners add '-ing' or extra 'to' after invitation and suggestion phrases. Remember: after 'Would you like to', 'Let's', and 'Why don't we', always use the BASE FORM of the verb — the simplest form with no changes.
commonTrap.wrong: Would you like to going to the park? / Let's to eat pizza. / Why don't we watching TV?
commonTrap.correct: Would you like to go to the park? / Let's eat pizza. / Why don't we watch TV?

sections.title: Reading Passage: Weekend Plans with Friends

content.context: It is Wednesday afternoon. Three friends — Mia, Tom, and Lily — are chatting in a group message about their plans for the weekend. Read their conversation to find out what they decide to do.
content.text:
Mia: Hi everyone! Do you have any plans for this Saturday? I'm free all day. Would you like to have lunch together?

Tom: That sounds great, Mia! I'd love to. Where do you want to go?

Mia: How about the new Italian restaurant on Park Street? I hear the pizza is really good.

Tom: Perfect! Let's meet there at 12:30 PM.

Lily: Hi guys! I'm sorry, I can't join you for lunch. I have an appointment at 12 PM. But I'm available after 3 PM. Why don't we watch a movie in the evening?

Mia: Good suggestion, Lily! There's a new comedy at the cinema. Let's go at 6 PM.

Tom: Sure, why not? I'd love to see it. Let's arrange to meet at the cinema at 5:45 PM.

Lily: Great! I'll be there. It's going to be a fun Saturday!

Mia: I'm so excited! See you both on Saturday!

highlights.text: Would you like to have lunch together?
highlights.note: This is a polite invitation using 'Would you like to + base verb'. Notice 'have' is in the base form.
'I'd love to' is a contraction of 'I would love to' — a warm way to accept an invitation.
'Let's + base verb' is used to make a suggestion. 'Meet' is the base form — no 'to' after 'Let's'.

highlights.text: I'm sorry, I can't join you
highlights.note: This is a polite way to decline an invitation. Notice the speaker gives a reason (an appointment).

highlights.text: Why don't we watch a movie
highlights.note: 'Why don't we + base verb' is another way to make a suggestion. 'Watch' is the base form.
A 'suggestion' is an idea you offer to someone. Lily makes a suggestion about watching a movie.
'Available' means you are free and can do something. Lily is available after 3 PM.
'Arrange' means to organize or set up a plan. Tom arranges to meet at the cinema.

gistQuestion.prompt: What is the main idea of this conversation?
options: Three friends are making plans to have lunch and watch a movie on Saturday.
Three friends are talking about their jobs and daily routines.
Three friends are planning a holiday trip to Italy.
gistQuestion.explanation: The conversation is about Mia, Tom, and Lily making plans for Saturday. They arrange to have lunch at a restaurant and watch a movie in the evening. The main idea is about making plans and invitations for the weekend.

detailQuestions.prompt: Where do Mia and Tom plan to have lunch?
options: At the new Italian restaurant on Park Street.
At Mia's house.
At a café near the cinema.
detailQuestions.explanation: Mia suggests 'the new Italian restaurant on Park Street' and Tom agrees by saying 'Perfect!' So they plan to have lunch at the Italian restaurant.

detailQuestions.prompt: Why can't Lily join Mia and Tom for lunch?
options: She has an appointment at 12 PM.
She doesn't like Italian food.
She is working all day Saturday.
detailQuestions.explanation: Lily says 'I have an appointment at 12 PM.' This is why she can't join them for lunch. She politely declines and then suggests a different activity for later.

detailQuestions.prompt: What time do the friends plan to meet at the cinema?
options: At 5:45 PM.
At 6:00 PM.
At 3:00 PM.
detailQuestions.explanation: Tom says 'Let's arrange to meet at the cinema at 5:45 PM.' The movie starts at 6 PM, but they agree to meet 15 minutes earlier at 5:45 PM.

detailQuestions.prompt: How does Tom respond to Mia's lunch invitation?
options: He accepts by saying 'That sounds great! I'd love to.'
He declines by saying 'I'm sorry, I'm busy.'
He suggests a different day.
detailQuestions.explanation: Tom responds with 'That sounds great, Mia! I'd love to.' These are both polite and enthusiastic ways to accept an invitation.

questions.question: In the passage, who makes the first invitation?
options: Mia
Tom
Lily
questions.explanation: Mia is the first person to make an invitation. She asks 'Would you like to have lunch together?' at the beginning of the conversation.

questions.question: Which phrase does Lily use to make a suggestion about the evening?
options: Why don't we watch a movie in the evening?
Would you like to watch a movie?
Let's have dinner together.
questions.answer: Why don't we watch a movie in the evening?
questions.explanation: Lily uses the suggestion pattern 'Why don't we + base verb?' She says 'Why don't we watch a movie in the evening?' to propose an evening activity.

questions.question: What does 'I'd love to' mean in the conversation?
options: It means 'I would love to' — a polite way to accept an invitation.
It means 'I don't want to' — a polite way to decline.
It means 'I am not sure' — a way to ask for more information.
questions.answer: It means 'I would love to' — a polite way to accept an invitation.
questions.explanation: 'I'd love to' is a contraction of 'I would love to.' It is a warm, enthusiastic way to say yes to an invitation. Tom uses it when he accepts Mia's lunch invitation.

questions.question: Which sentence correctly uses 'Let's' to make a suggestion?
options: Let's go to the park after lunch.
Let's to going to the park after lunch.
Let's goes to the park after lunch.
questions.answer: Let's go to the park after lunch.
questions.explanation: After 'Let's', we always use the base form of the verb. 'Let's go' is correct. 'Let's to going' adds an unnecessary 'to' and uses '-ing', and 'Let's goes' incorrectly adds '-s' to the verb.

questions.question: In the passage, Lily declines the lunch invitation politely. Which of these is also a polite way to decline an invitation?
options: I'd love to, but I can't. Maybe another time?
No. I don't want to go.
I'm not coming. Goodbye.
questions.answer: I'd love to, but I can't. Maybe another time?
questions.explanation: 'I'd love to, but I can't. Maybe another time?' is polite because it shows you want to say yes but have a reason you cannot. The other options are too direct and not polite in English social situations.

questions.question: According to the passage, what kind of movie are the friends going to watch?
options: A comedy.
An action movie.
A horror movie.
questions.explanation: Mia says 'There's a new comedy at the cinema.' A comedy is a funny movie. The friends agree to watch this new comedy on Saturday evening.

questions.question: Read this sentence: 'I'm available after 3 PM.' What does 'available' mean here?
options: Free and able to do something at that time.
Very tired and wanting to rest.
At work and unable to leave.
questions.answer: Free and able to do something at that time.
questions.explanation: 'Available' means you are free and can do something. When Lily says 'I'm available after 3 PM,' she means she is not busy after 3 PM and can join her friends for an activity.

content.summary: In this listening mission, you will hear two friends making plans to watch a movie together on the weekend. You will practise listening for key phrases used to invite someone, suggest a time or place, accept an invitation, and politely decline or offer an alternative. Pay close attention to question forms like 'Would you like to...?', 'How about...?', and 'Why don't we...?' as these are the most common ways to make suggestions and invitations at the A1 level. Also listen for how speakers agree, disagree politely, and confirm final plans.
learningObjectives: Identify key phrases for making invitations such as 'Would you like to...?' and 'Let's...'
Recognise how speakers suggest a time or place using 'How about...?' and 'Why don't we...?'
Understand how to politely decline an invitation and offer an alternative
Catch specific details like times, days, and places mentioned in a conversation about plans

keyPhrases.note: A polite way to invite someone to do something. Used at the start of an invitation.
A common way to accept a suggestion or invitation with enthusiasm.
Used to make a suggestion about a time, place, or activity.
A polite way to decline an invitation by giving a reason.
Used to suggest an alternative plan or idea to someone.
Used to suggest a meeting place. 'Let's' is short for 'let us' and is used for suggestions.
Used to confirm that a suggested time or plan is acceptable for you.
A friendly phrase to show you are excited about a future plan.

connectedSpeech.slow: Would you like to watch a movie?
connectedSpeech.fast: Wudjya like ta watch a movie?
connectedSpeech.slowIpa: /wʊd juː laɪk tuː wɒtʃ ə ˈmuːvi/
connectedSpeech.note: 'Would you' blends together to sound like 'wudjya' in fast speech. The word 'to' reduces to 'ta'. Listen for this very common pattern in invitations.
'How' and 'about' link together smoothly with no pause between them. The phrase sounds almost like one long word.
The 't' at the end of 'don't' often disappears before 'we', so it sounds like 'donwe'. The word 'at' reduces to a quick 'ut' sound.

connectedSpeech.slow: I am looking forward to it.
connectedSpeech.note: 'I am' contracts to 'I'm'. The 'g' in 'looking' is often dropped in casual speech, becoming 'lookin'. The word 'to' reduces to 'ta'.
'See you' blends into 'seeya' in natural speech. This is extremely common in casual goodbyes and when confirming plans.

sections.title: Audio Dialogue: Planning a Movie Night

content.context: Sarah and David are friends. Sarah calls David to invite him to watch a movie this Saturday. They discuss what time to meet, where to go, and which movie to see. Listen carefully to how they make suggestions, accept ideas, politely decline, and confirm their final plan.
content.audioPrompt: Listen carefully to the following dialogue between two friends making plans for the weekend.

lines.speaker: Sarah
lines.text: Hi David! Would you like to watch a movie this Saturday?
lines.translation: Hai David! Apakah kamu mau menonton film Sabtu ini?

lines.speaker: David
lines.text: That sounds great! What time are you thinking?
lines.translation: Kedengarannya bagus! Jam berapa kamu pikirkan?

lines.speaker: Sarah
lines.text: How about 5 PM? Let's meet at the cinema.
lines.translation: Bagaimana kalau jam 5 sore? Ayo kita bertemu di bioskop.

lines.speaker: David
lines.text: I'm sorry, I'm busy at 5. Why don't we meet at 7 PM instead?
lines.translation: Maaf, aku sibuk jam 5. Kenapa kita tidak bertemu jam 7 malam saja?

lines.speaker: Sarah
lines.text: Perfect! 7 PM works for me. Which movie would you like to see?
lines.translation: Sempurna! Jam 7 malam cocok untukku. Film mana yang ingin kamu tonton?

lines.speaker: David
lines.text: Let's watch the new action movie. I'll buy the tickets online.
lines.translation: Ayo kita tonton film aksi yang baru. Aku akan beli tiketnya online.

lines.speaker: Sarah
lines.text: Great idea! See you on Saturday at 7!
lines.translation: Ide bagus! Sampai jumpa Sabtu jam 7!

lines.speaker: David
lines.text: See you then! I'm looking forward to it.

lines.speaker: Sarah
lines.text: Me too! Don't forget to bring some snacks!
lines.translation: Aku juga! Jangan lupa bawa camilan!

lines.speaker: David
lines.text: Sure! I'll bring popcorn. See you Saturday!
lines.translation: Tentu! Aku akan bawa popcorn. Sampai jumpa Sabtu!

content.summary: In this writing blueprint, you will learn how to write invitations, make suggestions, and respond politely. You will use three important patterns: 'Would you like to...?' to invite someone, 'Let's...' and 'Why don't we...?' to make suggestions, and polite phrases to accept or decline. These are very useful for making plans with friends, family, or classmates. Let's learn step by step!

blueprintItems.title: Invite Someone with 'Would you like to...?'
blueprintItems.formula: Would you like to + verb (base form) + details?
blueprintItems.example: Would you like to come to my birthday party on Saturday?

blueprintItems.title: Make a Suggestion with 'Let's...' or 'Why don't we...?'
blueprintItems.formula: Let's + verb (base form) + details. / Why don't we + verb (base form) + details?
blueprintItems.example: Let's meet at the park at 3 PM. / Why don't we go to the cinema tonight?

blueprintItems.title: Accept an Invitation Politely
blueprintItems.example: That sounds great! I will be there at 3 PM.

blueprintItems.title: Decline an Invitation Politely
blueprintItems.example: I'm sorry, I'm busy on Saturday. Maybe another time?

mechanicsRules.rule: Always use a question mark (?) at the end of invitations and suggestions that are questions.
mechanicsRules.badExample: Would you like to join us.
mechanicsRules.goodExample: Would you like to join us?
mechanicsRules.why: Invitations with 'Would you like to...?' and suggestions with 'Why don't we...?' are questions. Questions always need a question mark at the end.

mechanicsRules.rule: Always capitalize the first word of a sentence and the word 'I'.
mechanicsRules.badExample: i'd love to! let's go together.
mechanicsRules.goodExample: I'd love to! Let's go together.
mechanicsRules.why: Every sentence starts with a capital letter. The pronoun 'I' is always capitalized in English.

mechanicsRules.rule: Use an apostrophe correctly in contractions like 'Let's', 'I'd', 'don't', and 'can't'.
mechanicsRules.badExample: Lets go to the park. I d love to, but I cant.
mechanicsRules.goodExample: Let's go to the park. I'd love to, but I can't.
mechanicsRules.why: 'Let's' is short for 'Let us'. 'I'd' is short for 'I would'. 'Don't' is short for 'do not'. 'Can't' is short for 'cannot'. The apostrophe shows that letters are missing.

mechanicsRules.rule: Use a comma after polite phrases like 'I'm sorry' when followed by a reason.
mechanicsRules.badExample: I'm sorry I'm busy on Friday.
mechanicsRules.goodExample: I'm sorry, I'm busy on Friday.
mechanicsRules.why: A comma after 'I'm sorry' makes the sentence clearer and more polite. It separates the apology from the reason.

mechanicsChallenges.keyRule: Use apostrophes in contractions: 'Let's' and 'I'd'. Separate two complete ideas with a period. Capitalize the first word of each sentence.

guidedLabChallenges.title: Challenge 1: Invite a Friend to Your Event
guidedLabChallenges.instruction: Write a short message to invite your friend to an event. Use 'Would you like to...?' to make the invitation. Tell your friend what the event is, when it is, and where it is. Write at least 3 sentences.
guidedLabChallenges.example: Hi Anna! Would you like to come to my birthday party? It is on Saturday at 4 PM. The party is at my house. We will have cake and games. I hope you can come!

guidedLabChallenges.title: Challenge 2: Make Plans for the Weekend
guidedLabChallenges.instruction: Write a short conversation between you and a friend. You make a suggestion using 'Let's...' or 'Why don't we...?' and your friend responds. Your friend can accept or decline politely. Write at least 4 lines of dialogue. Use the format: 'You: ...' and 'Friend: ...'
guidedLabChallenges.example:
You: Hi Tom! Why don't we go to the park this Sunday?
Friend: That sounds great! What time?
You: Let's meet at 10 AM at the park entrance.
Friend: Sure, why not? See you there!

guidedLabChallenges.title: Challenge 3: Accept and Decline Invitations
guidedLabChallenges.instruction:
Your friend sends you two invitations. Write a polite reply for each one. For the first invitation, accept it and say something nice. For the second invitation, decline politely and give a reason. Each reply should be at least 2 sentences.

Invitation 1: 'Would you like to have lunch with me on Wednesday?'
Invitation 2: 'Would you like to go shopping on Friday evening?'
guidedLabChallenges.example:
Reply 1: I'd love to! Let's meet at the Italian restaurant at 12 PM. I can't wait!

Reply 2: I'm sorry, I can't go on Friday. I have a family dinner. Maybe another time?

practicumQuestions.prompt: Your school is having a fun day next Saturday. Write a short invitation message to your friend. Include: what the event is, when and where it is, and use 'Would you like to...?' to invite your friend. Write at least 3 sentences.
practicumQuestions.criteria: Uses 'Would you like to...?' correctly with a base form verb. Includes details about the event (what, when, where). Sentences start with capital letters and end with correct punctuation. The message is friendly and clear. At least 3 complete sentences.
practicumQuestions.sampleGoodAnswer: Hi Maria! My school is having a fun day next Saturday. Would you like to come with me? It starts at 9 AM at the school hall. There will be games, food, and music. I hope you can come!

practicumQuestions.prompt: You want to make plans with your friend for this weekend. Write a short message. Make at least one suggestion using 'Let's...' and one suggestion using 'Why don't we...?'. Include the day and time. Write at least 4 sentences.
practicumQuestions.criteria: Uses 'Let's + base form verb' correctly in at least one sentence. Uses 'Why don't we + base form verb...?' correctly in at least one sentence. Includes a specific day and time. Correct use of apostrophes in contractions. Proper capitalization and punctuation throughout. At least 4 complete sentences.
practicumQuestions.sampleGoodAnswer: Hi Jake! Are you free this weekend? Let's go to the new pizza restaurant on Saturday. Why don't we meet at 6 PM at the bus stop? We can eat pizza and talk. It will be fun!

practicumQuestions.prompt: Read this invitation from your friend: 'Hi! Would you like to go to the zoo with me on Sunday? We can see the animals and have a picnic. Let me know!' Write two different replies. In Reply 1, accept the invitation politely. In Reply 2, decline the invitation politely and give a reason. Each reply should be at least 2 sentences.
practicumQuestions.criteria: Reply 1 uses a polite acceptance phrase such as 'That sounds great!', 'I'd love to!', or 'Sure, why not?'. Reply 2 uses a polite refusal phrase such as 'I'm sorry, I'm busy', 'I'd love to, but I can't', or 'Maybe another time?'. Reply 2 includes a clear reason for declining. Correct use of apostrophes, capitalization, and punctuation. Each reply has at least 2 complete sentences.
practicumQuestions.sampleGoodAnswer:
Reply 1: That sounds great! I'd love to go to the zoo with you. Let's meet at the entrance at 10 AM. I can't wait to see the animals!

Reply 2: I'm sorry, I can't go on Sunday. I have to visit my grandparents. I'd love to, but I'm busy. Maybe we can go another time?

subModules.title: Speaking Lab: Making Plans, Suggestions & Invitations

content.summary: In this Speaking Lab, you will practise how to invite friends, make plans, suggest times and places, and politely accept or decline invitations. You will learn the correct intonation for questions like 'Would you like to...?' and 'How about...?' and practise stress patterns in key vocabulary such as 'tomorrow', 'together', 'suggestion', and 'invitation'. Good pronunciation and friendly intonation will help you sound polite and natural when making plans in English.
content.audioGuidance: When you make an invitation or suggestion, your voice should rise at the end of yes/no questions like 'Would you like to come?' but fall at the end of statements like 'That sounds great!' For 'Wh-' suggestions like 'Why don't we meet at 1 PM?', use a gentle falling tone at the end. Speak slowly and clearly. Smile when you speak — it naturally makes your voice sound warmer and more inviting.

pillars.name: Invitation Intonation
pillars.explanation: When you ask 'Would you like to have lunch together?', your voice should gently rise on the last word. This rising tone shows that you are asking a question and being polite. Practise saying the sentence and lifting your voice on 'together?' to sound friendly and inviting.

pillars.name: Suggestion Stress
pillars.target: Correct word stress in suggestion phrases
pillars.explanation: In phrases like 'How about 12:30?' and 'Why don't we meet at 1 PM?', stress the key information words: the time, place, or activity. For example, say 'How about TWELVE THIRTY?' with emphasis on the time. This helps your listener understand the most important part of your suggestion.

pillars.name: Polite Acceptance & Refusal
pillars.target: Natural rhythm when accepting or declining
pillars.explanation: When you accept an invitation, use a warm falling tone: 'That sounds GREAT!' When you decline, start with 'I'm sorry' using a soft, sympathetic tone, then give your reason: 'I'm SORry, I have a MEETing.' Practise pausing briefly after 'I'm sorry' to sound genuinely polite before explaining why you cannot come.

pillars.name: Connected Speech
pillars.target: Linking words smoothly in common plan-making phrases
pillars.explanation: In natural speech, words connect together. 'Would you' sounds like 'Wʊdʒə', 'Let's meet at' sounds like 'lets-MEE-dat', and 'looking forward to it' sounds like 'LOOK-ing-FOR-wəd-tə-it'. Practise linking these words together so your speech flows naturally instead of sounding word-by-word.

stressPairs.shiftExplanation: The stress shifts from the second syllable in 'inVITE' to the third syllable in 'inviTAtion'. When a word gets the suffix '-tion', the stress usually moves to the syllable just before it.

In 'sugGEST', the stress is on the second syllable. In 'sugGEStion', the stress stays on 'GES' because the '-tion' ending is unstressed. The rhythm stays similar, but notice the extra syllable at the end.
The stress moves from 'VAIL' in 'aVAILable' to 'BIL' in 'availaBILity'. When the suffix '-ity' is added, the stress shifts to the syllable right before it. This is a common pattern in English.

In the single word 'toMORrow', the stress is on 'MOR'. When combined with 'afternoon' in a phrase, 'toMORrow' keeps its stress, and 'afterNOON' adds a second strong stress. Practise saying both stressed syllables clearly.

drills.targetText: Would you like to have lunch together?
drills.phonetic: /wʊd juː laɪk tə hæv lʌntʃ təˈɡeðər/
drills.focus: Rising intonation on yes/no invitation questions
drills.hint: Let your voice gently rise on the word 'together' at the end. This rising tone makes it sound like a polite question, not a command.

drills.focus: Stress on the time to highlight the suggestion
drills.hint: Stress the time '12:30' clearly. Say 'How about' quickly and then slow down on 'twelve thirty' so your listener catches the important information.

drills.targetText: Let's meet at the Italian restaurant near the office.
drills.phonetic: /lets miːt æt ðə ɪˈtæliən ˈrestərɒnt nɪər ðə ˈɒfɪs/
drills.focus: Linking words and stressing location nouns
drills.hint: Link 'Let's meet at' smoothly as one phrase: 'lets-MEET-at'. Then stress 'Italian', 'restaurant', and 'office' because these are the key location words.

drills.targetText: I'm sorry, I have a meeting at 12:30.
drills.phonetic: /aɪm ˈsɒri aɪ hæv ə ˈmiːtɪŋ æt twelv ˈθɜːrti/
drills.hint: Say 'I'm sorry' with a soft, lower tone to show you feel bad. Then pause briefly before giving your reason. This makes your refusal sound polite and genuine.

drills.targetText: Why don't we meet at 1 PM instead?
drills.phonetic: /waɪ doʊnt wiː miːt æt wʌn piː ɛm ɪnˈsted/
drills.hint: This is a suggestion, not a real question, so use a gentle falling tone at the end on 'instead'. Stress '1 PM' and 'instead' to highlight your alternative idea.

drills.targetText: That's perfect! 1 PM works for me.
drills.phonetic: /ðæts ˈpɜːrfɪkt wʌn piː ɛm wɜːrks fɔːr miː/
drills.hint: Say 'That's perfect!' with energy and a falling tone to show you are happy. Stress 'perfect' and 'works' to confirm your agreement clearly.

drills.focus: Natural rhythm and linking in a common phrase
drills.hint: Link 'looking forward to it' smoothly. Stress 'LOOK' and 'FOR' and reduce 'to it' to a quick 'tə-it'. This phrase should flow as one natural unit.

roleplay.context: You are practising with Mr. Khoirul. You want to invite him to have lunch together tomorrow. You need to suggest a time and a place, respond to his counter-suggestion, and confirm the plan politely. Use invitation phrases like 'Would you like to...?', suggestion phrases like 'How about...?', and polite responses.

turns.speaker: Mr. Khoirul
turns.text: Hello! How are you doing today?

turns.speaker: You
turns.text: Hi Mr. Khoirul! I'm good, thanks. Would you like to have lunch together tomorrow?
turns.translation: Hai Pak Khoirul! Saya baik, terima kasih. Apakah Anda mau makan siang bersama besok?

turns.speaker: Mr. Khoirul
turns.text: That sounds wonderful! What time are you available?
turns.translation: Kedengarannya bagus! Jam berapa kamu tersedia?

turns.speaker: You
turns.text: How about 12:30 PM? Let's meet at the Italian restaurant near the office.
turns.translation: Bagaimana kalau jam 12:30 siang? Ayo bertemu di restoran Italia dekat kantor.

turns.speaker: Mr. Khoirul
turns.text: I'm sorry, I have a meeting at 12:30. Why don't we meet at 1 PM instead?
turns.translation: Maaf, saya ada rapat jam 12:30. Bagaimana kalau kita bertemu jam 1 siang saja?

turns.speaker: You
turns.text: That's perfect! 1 PM works for me. See you tomorrow!
turns.translation: Sempurna! Jam 1 siang cocok untuk saya. Sampai jumpa besok!

turns.speaker: Mr. Khoirul
turns.text: Excellent! I'm looking forward to it. Have a great day!
turns.translation: Luar biasa! Saya menantikannya. Semoga harimu menyenangkan!

turns.speaker: You
turns.translation: Anda juga, Pak Khoirul! Selamat tinggal!

practicumQuestions.instruction: Tell a short story about a time you invited a friend to do something together. Follow the three story points below. Speak clearly and use invitation and plan-making phrases you have learned.
practicumQuestions.audioPrompt: Now, I want you to tell me a story. Think about a time you invited a friend to go somewhere or do something together. What did you suggest? What did your friend say? Tell me the story using the three points on your screen.
storyPoints: Say who you invited and what activity you suggested (e.g., 'I invited my friend to go to the cinema.')
Explain when and where you planned to meet (e.g., 'I suggested meeting at 5 PM at the mall.')
Tell me if your friend accepted or declined, and what happened next (e.g., 'She said yes, and we had a great time!')
practicumQuestions.targetSentence: Last week, I invited my friend to go to the cinema. I suggested meeting at 5 PM at the mall. She said yes, and we watched a really fun movie together.
practicumQuestions.phonetic: /lɑːst wiːk aɪ ɪnˈvaɪtɪd maɪ frend tə ɡoʊ tə ðə ˈsɪnəmə/
practicumQuestions.hint: Use past tense for your story: 'I invited', 'I suggested', 'She said'. Keep your sentences short and clear.
practicumQuestions.explanation: This storytelling task practises using invitation and suggestion vocabulary in a natural narrative. You should use past tense forms and connect your ideas with simple linking words like 'and', 'so', and 'then'.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Tell a short story about a time someone invited you to something but you had to say no. Follow the three story points below. Use polite refusal phrases.
practicumQuestions.audioPrompt: Now tell me about a time when someone invited you to do something, but you could not go. What did they invite you to? Why did you say no? What happened after that? Use the three points on your screen.
storyPoints: Say who invited you and what the invitation was (e.g., 'My colleague invited me to a birthday party.')
Explain why you could not go and how you declined politely (e.g., 'I said I was sorry, but I had a family dinner.')
Tell what happened next — did you make a different plan? (e.g., 'We decided to have coffee the next day instead.')
practicumQuestions.targetSentence: My colleague invited me to a birthday party on Saturday. I said I was sorry, but I had a family dinner that evening. We decided to have coffee together on Sunday instead.
practicumQuestions.phonetic: /maɪ ˈkɒliːɡ ɪnˈvaɪtɪd miː tə ə ˈbɜːrθdeɪ ˈpɑːrti/
practicumQuestions.hint: When you decline, say 'I'm sorry, but...' first, then give your reason. This sounds polite. End your story by telling what you did instead.
practicumQuestions.explanation: This task practises polite refusal language and making alternative plans. Using 'I'm sorry, but...' followed by a reason is the standard polite way to decline at A1 level. Suggesting an alternative shows good communication skills.

practicumQuestions.instruction: You will have a phone call with your friend Lisa. You want to invite her to see a movie this weekend. Suggest a day, time, and place. If she cannot make it, offer an alternative.
practicumQuestions.audioPrompt: Ring ring! Your friend Lisa is calling you. Answer the phone and invite her to see a movie this weekend. You need to agree on a day, time, and place.
practicumQuestions.scenarioContext: You are calling your friend Lisa on the phone. You want to invite her to watch a new movie at the cinema this weekend. You need to suggest a specific day and time. If Lisa says she is busy, you should suggest a different time. Be friendly and polite.
practicumQuestions.characterRole: Lisa — a friendly colleague who is sometimes busy on weekends but loves movies. She may suggest a different time if your first suggestion does not work.
practicumQuestions.targetSentence: Hi Lisa! Would you like to go to the cinema this Saturday? How about the 3 PM show?
practicumQuestions.phonetic: /haɪ ˈliːsə wʊd juː laɪk tə ɡoʊ tə ðə ˈsɪnəmə ðɪs ˈsætərdeɪ/
practicumQuestions.hint: Start with a greeting, then use 'Would you like to...?' to make your invitation. If Lisa says no, try 'How about...?' with a new time.
practicumQuestions.explanation: This roleplay practises making invitations using 'Would you like to...?' and suggesting alternatives with 'How about...?' These are essential A1 phrases for social planning.

practicumQuestions.instruction: You will receive a call from your neighbour Tom. He wants to invite you to a barbecue at his house. You are free and want to accept. Ask what time and what you should bring.
practicumQuestions.audioPrompt: Your neighbour Tom is calling you. He has something to invite you to. Listen to his invitation and respond politely. Accept his invitation and ask for details.
practicumQuestions.scenarioContext: Your neighbour Tom is calling to invite you to a barbecue at his house this Sunday. You are free and happy to go. You need to accept politely, ask what time the barbecue starts, and offer to bring something like drinks or salad.
practicumQuestions.characterRole: Tom — a friendly neighbour who is having a barbecue this Sunday afternoon. He is excited and wants you to come. He will tell you the time and happily accept your offer to bring something.
practicumQuestions.targetSentence: That sounds great, Tom! I'd love to come. What time does it start? Can I bring anything?
practicumQuestions.phonetic: /ðæt saʊndz ɡreɪt tɒm aɪd lʌv tə kʌm wɒt taɪm dʌz ɪt stɑːrt/
practicumQuestions.hint: To accept happily, say 'That sounds great!' or 'I'd love to come!' Then ask practical questions like 'What time?' and 'Can I bring anything?'
practicumQuestions.explanation: This roleplay practises accepting invitations enthusiastically and asking follow-up questions. Offering to bring something is a polite social habit that shows good manners in English-speaking cultures.

practicumQuestions.instruction: You will call your classmate Maria to make plans for studying together. You need to suggest a day, time, and place to study. Agree on a final plan.
practicumQuestions.audioPrompt: You need to study for your English test next week. Call your classmate Maria and suggest studying together. You need to decide when and where to meet.
practicumQuestions.scenarioContext: You have an English test next week and you want to study with your classmate Maria. You are calling her to suggest studying together at the library or a café. You need to agree on a day (this week), a time, and a place that works for both of you.
practicumQuestions.characterRole: Maria — a classmate who also wants to study for the English test. She is free on Wednesday and Thursday evenings. She prefers studying at the library because it is quiet.
practicumQuestions.targetSentence: Hi Maria! Would you like to study together for the English test? How about Wednesday evening at the library?
practicumQuestions.phonetic: /haɪ məˈriːə wʊd juː laɪk tə ˈstʌdi təˈɡeðər fɔːr ðə ˈɪŋɡlɪʃ test/
practicumQuestions.hint: Use 'Would you like to study together?' for the invitation. Then suggest a specific day and place with 'How about...?' Be ready to agree or suggest alternatives.
practicumQuestions.explanation: This roleplay practises making plans for a specific activity. At A1 level, you should be able to suggest a time and place, and negotiate simple changes if the other person is not available.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Your boss Mr. Khoirul invites you to a team dinner on Friday. You cannot go because you have a family event. Decline politely and suggest meeting for coffee next week instead.
practicumQuestions.audioPrompt: Mr. Khoirul is calling you about a team dinner this Friday evening. Unfortunately, you have a family event and cannot attend. You need to decline politely and suggest an alternative plan.
practicumQuestions.scenarioContext: Mr. Khoirul, your boss, is inviting you to a team dinner at a restaurant this Friday at 7 PM. You cannot go because you have a family birthday party that evening. You need to decline politely, explain your reason briefly, and suggest having coffee together next week as an alternative.
practicumQuestions.characterRole: Mr. Khoirul — your friendly boss who is organising a team dinner. He understands when people are busy and appreciates polite explanations. He will be happy if you suggest meeting another time.
practicumQuestions.targetSentence: Thank you for the invitation, Mr. Khoirul. I'm sorry, but I have a family event on Friday. Would you like to have coffee next week instead?
practicumQuestions.phonetic: /θæŋk juː fɔːr ðə ɪnvɪˈteɪʃən aɪm ˈsɒri bʌt aɪ hæv ə ˈfæməli ɪˈvent ɒn ˈfraɪdeɪ/
practicumQuestions.hint: Start by thanking him: 'Thank you for the invitation.' Then say 'I'm sorry, but...' and give your reason. Finally, suggest an alternative: 'Would you like to... instead?'
practicumQuestions.explanation: This roleplay practises the full cycle of politely declining an invitation: thanking, apologising, giving a reason, and suggesting an alternative. This is an important social skill even at A1 level.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Say the following sentence out loud. Focus on using the correct vocabulary for making suggestions and invitations.
practicumQuestions.audioPrompt: Please say this sentence clearly. Pay attention to the key vocabulary words for making plans.
practicumQuestions.targetSentence: Why don't we go to the park this afternoon?
practicumQuestions.phonetic: /waɪ doʊnt wiː ɡoʊ tə ðə pɑːrk ðɪs ˌæftərˈnuːn/
practicumQuestions.hint: The phrase 'Why don't we' is a common way to make a suggestion. It means the same as 'Let's' or 'How about'. Say it as one smooth phrase: 'why-DONT-we'.
practicumQuestions.explanation: 'Why don't we...?' is a friendly suggestion phrase at A1 level. Other similar phrases include 'How about...?', 'Let's...', and 'Shall we...?' Knowing multiple ways to suggest activities makes your English more natural and flexible.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Say the following sentence out loud. Focus on the correct grammar structure for polite invitations using 'Would you like to + verb'.
practicumQuestions.audioPrompt: Please say this sentence. Be careful with the grammar: 'Would you like to' is always followed by the base form of the verb.
practicumQuestions.targetSentence: Would you like to come to my birthday party next Saturday?
practicumQuestions.phonetic: /wʊd juː laɪk tə kʌm tə maɪ ˈbɜːrθdeɪ ˈpɑːrti nekst ˈsætərdeɪ/
practicumQuestions.hint: The structure is: 'Would you like to + base verb'. Always use the base form: 'come' (not 'coming' or 'came'). Say 'Would you' quickly as 'wʊdʒə' in natural speech.
practicumQuestions.explanation: The grammar pattern 'Would you like to + infinitive' is the most polite way to make invitations at A1 level. The base verb (infinitive without 'to') always follows 'like to'. Common examples: 'Would you like to come?', 'Would you like to join us?', 'Would you like to have dinner?'

practicumQuestions.instruction: Say both words and notice how the stress shifts. First say 'invite' with stress on the second syllable, then say 'invitation' with stress on the third syllable.
practicumQuestions.audioPrompt: Listen carefully to the stress pattern. Say 'inVITE' — the stress is on 'VITE'. Now say 'inviTAtion' — the stress moves to 'TA'. Practise both words and feel the stress shift.
practicumQuestions.targetSentence: Thank you for the invitation. I would like to invite you to dinner.
practicumQuestions.phonetic: /θæŋk juː fɔːr ðə ˌɪnvɪˈteɪʃən aɪ wʊd laɪk tə ɪnˈvaɪt juː tə ˈdɪnər/
practicumQuestions.hint: In 'inVITE', clap on 'VITE'. In 'inviTAtion', clap on 'TA'. The stress shifts forward when the word gets longer. Practise: in-VITE → in-vi-TA-tion.
practicumQuestions.explanation: Stress shift is common when verbs become nouns with the suffix '-tion'. The verb 'inVITE' has stress on the second syllable, but the noun 'inviTAtion' shifts the stress to the third syllable (just before '-tion'). This pattern also applies to: sugGEST → sugGEStion, celeBRATE → celeBRAtion.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Say the following two sentences. The first is a yes/no invitation question — use RISING intonation. The second is a suggestion — use FALLING intonation.
practicumQuestions.audioPrompt: Practise the difference between rising and falling intonation. For the invitation question 'Would you like to join us?', your voice goes UP at the end. For the suggestion 'Let's meet at the café', your voice goes DOWN at the end. Say both sentences now.
practicumQuestions.targetSentence: Would you like to join us? ↗ Let's meet at the café. ↘
practicumQuestions.phonetic: /wʊd juː laɪk tə dʒɔɪn ʌs ↗ lets miːt æt ðə kæˈfeɪ ↘/
practicumQuestions.hint: Yes/no questions (like invitations with 'Would you like to...?') use RISING intonation ↗ because you are waiting for an answer. Statements and suggestions (like 'Let's meet at...') use FALLING intonation ↘ because you are giving a clear plan.
practicumQuestions.explanation: In English, rising intonation (↗) signals a yes/no question — the speaker wants a response. Falling intonation (↘) signals a statement, command, or confident suggestion. When making invitations, 'Would you like to...?' rises because it is a question. 'Let's...' falls because it is a direct suggestion. Mastering this difference makes your English sound natural and easy to understand.
